IBS  
12 June 2026     The Chartered Accountant Student  
Effective decision-making requires a holistic view of business, where different functional areas are understood as 
interconnected rather than operating in isolation. Reflecting this principle, this issue presents a pharmaceutical case 
study based on realistic challenges and practical problems commonly faced by the industry. The objective is to encourage 
integrated thinking, analytical problem-solving, and leadership-oriented decision-making by exposing students to 
complex business situations that require balanced and strategic responses.
“Competitive strategy is about being different. It means deliberately choosing a different set of activities to 
deliver a unique mix of value.”
	
— Michel E. Porter 
CA FINAL - PAPER 6: INTEGRATED BUSINESS SOLUTIONS (IBS) 
Company Background
Revixa Pharmaceutical Limited (RPL) is a renowned pharmaceutical company, with its headquarters in Hyderabad, Telangana. 
Dr. Shankar Prasad founded this company in Nalgonda near Hyderabad in the year 1995. The enterprising scientist started the 
business as a small private company manufacturing generic medicines for minor ailments. Over the years it has grown into a large 
company treating a broad spectrum of healthcare needs; Their diverse portfolio that includes both branded and generic drugs for 
aliments related cardiology, gastroenterology, diabetology, oncology, ophthalmology, dermatology, nephrology, respiratory diseases, 
over-the-counter medicines among others. They also manufacture Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs). These are the key 
drug formulation / molecules needed to manufacture medicines. APIs are used both for in-house production as well as sold to 
external third parties.
RPL started out with operations primarily focused on the Indian domestic market. In recent years, the company has been working 
on establishing its presence globally by increasing its market reach in other countries. Exports from India reach almost 30 countries 
spread across North America, Europe and Asia.  Therefore, revenue from exports has steadily increased over the years. They now 
contribute almost 45% share in total revenue of the company. In the overseas market USA contributes almost 60% of the revenue 
generated from exports.
The company has many subsidiaries, each focusing on a specific area of therapeutic care. It has manufacturing facilities in Nalgonda, 
Telangana and Vishakhapatnam, Andra Pradesh. RPL ranks among the top 10 pharmaceutical companies in India in terms of market 
capitalization. Currently, it does not have manufacturing facilities outside India. To gain credibility globally, its Executive Chairman 
Dr. Shankar Prasad believes that science should be at the heart of the company’s operations. RPL has 2 laboratories in Telangana 
that focus on research and development in areas of therapeutic care that form part of the company’s overall vision and long-term 
strategy.  
Revixa Pharmaceutical Limited has a vision to transform lives globally using science to deliver effective and affordable 
healthcare solutions. With a keen sense of purpose, the company has been working to enhance healthcare standards by producing 
high quality medicines that improve patient care and drive better patient outcomes. The mission of the company is to leverage its 
product portfolio of both generic and branded drugs to cater to growing demand across diverse markets. This includes forging 
strategic alliances to strengthen the product portfolio while improving access to affordable medicines for the public across the 
world. It wishes to be a trusted partner that strives for profitable growth while building a sustainable, high quality product portfolio.
The board comprises diverse groups of individuals whose valuable experience, expertise, and oversight can be leveraged to enhance 
the company’s performance. They are individuals involved in various sectors and have expertise in pharmaceutical and healthcare 
industry. This diversity is crucial for the company’s corporate governance and decision-making process. Refer Annexure 2.
Board of Directors
Revixa Pharmaceutical Limited 

 IBS
The Chartered Accountant Student     June 2026 13
Exports have become vital for the company’s operations. Recently, the United States government proposed significant policy reforms 
aimed at strengthening its domestic economy. Among these measures, it has been proposed that a 100% tariff shall be imposed on 
imports of medicines and pharmaceutical products manufactured in other countries. Refer Annexure 1 for details of the discussion 
relating to this policy.
The developments are reason of concern for RPL. Dr. Shankar Prasad has called a meeting with the Board of Directors to discuss 
these developments. Among the many opinions that were discussed in the board meeting, the one that was most favored was given 
by Mr. Namansh Desai. 
Given his experience in working across industries and markets, he has been requested to write a brief about the market conditions in 
the African subcontinent. Refer Annexure 4 for details of the strategic brief shared by Mr. Naman Desai.
Mr. Aarav Singh had proposed an alternative strategy, which was extensively deliberated upon by the board but was eventually not 
approved. He stated, 
RPL has manufacturing facilities in Nalgonda, a city near Hyderabad. It has another manufacturing facility in Vishakhapatnam, 
Andra Pradesh. Currently, Dr. Yuvraj V Giri, has always encouraged the research and development team to pursue various projects 
that can lead to the discovery of newer or improved drug formulations. While many of these fail, there are few that fructify and earn 
the company the distinction of holding a patent for that particular drug formulation. RPL has the creditable achievement of owning 
12 patents. These patents are then used to produced drugs, which are known as patented drugs. Since many of these drugs improve 
treatment of various illness or bring newer cure for many ailments, they are highly coveted in the market. The patented drugs provide 
the company ‘first mover advantage’ in the market and serves as a product differentiator in a highly competitive market. RPL also 
enters into strategic alliances that provides it with access to technical knowhow to strengthen its product portfolio. While a patent is 
indeed unique in its innovation, it need not always be commercially viable. The company needs to constantly monitor the profitability 
achieved for commercial viability of its products.
Technical collaboration with Seek Care Corporation (S) Japan for launch of “Neucare” for liver cancer treatment 
On 1 April 2024, RPL entered into a technical collaboration agreement with Seek Care Corporation (SCC), a Japanese pharmaceutical 
company, to obtain the requisite technical know-how for manufacturing a generic drug named “Neucare”, used in the treatment of 
liver cancer. This partnership enabled RPL to enter a therapeutic segment that it had not catered to previously. For the use of the 
know-how over a period of five years, RPL paid a consideration of R27 crores.
“Neucare” is manufactured in the form of tablets. At the time of collaboration, SCC provided a projected production plan covering 
the next five years. The drug was launched during F.Y. 2024-25, and RPL successfully achieved the target production for the first 
year. During F.Y. 2025-26, the company observed stronger-than-expected market demand, prompting a revision of the production 
estimates from F.Y. 2025-26 onwards.
Initially, the production estimates were 8,00,000 tablets for F.Y. 2024-25, 10,00,000 tablets for FY 2025-26, and 12,00,000 tablets each 
for F.Y. 2026-27, F.Y. 2027-28 and F.Y. 2028-29, aggregating to 54,00,000 tablets over the five-year period. After reviewing the market 
trends, the estimates were revised upward to 11,00,000 tablets for F.Y. 2025-26 and 13,20,000 tablets per year for F.Y. 2026-27 through 
F.Y. 2028-29, resulting in a revised total expected production of 50,60,000 tablets over the remaining four years.
Monetization of asset by sale of patent of its health supplement “Flex Fit” to Healthy Planet Limited 
In F.Y. 2025-26, RPL purchased a patent to manufacture a health supplement drink “Flex Fit” which is expected to be a source of 
net cash inflows for at least 15 years. However, after acquisition the management of RPL is unsure if it can scale up and optimize 
production of Flex Fit in the long run such that it can get maximum revenue and profits. Therefore, the management decided to sell 
the patent to a willing buyer. Accordingly, Healthy Planet Limited has committed to purchase the patent in 5 years’ time at 60% of the 
patent’s fair value at the date it was acquired. On its part, RPL also intends to sell the patent in 5 years’ time.
“We have faced similar situations particularly in electronics industry. With respect to exports, RPL is highly concentrated in USA. It 
derives approximately 27% of its total revenue from this market alone. Negative impact of tariffs will hurt out financially. We need 
to mitigate this impact through several measures. We may need to lobby and negotiate to influence the US government to arrive at a 
more reasonable policy for the industry. It requires industry leaders from India and across the world to meet with the government to 
negotiate favorable terms. All this will take time, with results remaining uncertain. Therefore, it would then make sense to increase 
our footprint across the World. For example, after Asia, Africa is the second most populous continent. It would make good business 
sense to expand our operations there.  RPL already has a well-established product portfolio. Therefore, we can build alternate markets 
with our portfolio to generate revenue. This will mitigate the risk of concentration on a single market for export revenue.  Given the 
potential of capturing a huge market in Africa, in the long run RPL can even consider setting up some manufacturing facilities there.” 
“Instead of concentrating solely on medicines, the company should diversify into allied sectors such as medical devices. The medical 
devices industry is itself a multi-billion-dollar sector offering significant opportunities for expansion and growth. Demand for 
products such as electronic medical equipment, disposables and consumables, implants, and surgical instruments is rising rapidly 
alongside the growth of the healthcare industry. Compared to the pharmaceutical sector, the impact of public policy in this industry 
is relatively lower and the regulatory environment is less stringent. Diversification into such sectors can also support better risk 
management and long-term business sustainability.”
Navigating Uncertain Global Conditions
Strategy for Product Portfolio Management

IBS  
14 June 2026     The Chartered Accountant Student  
Mr. Mohan Giri has given an interview in the Strategy Focus magazine about RPL’s strategy to survive in a competitive market. Refer 
Annexure 3 for excerpts of this interview with renowned business journalist Lara Michael.
RPL’s Strategy to Survive in a Competitive Market
Since the company is working in a highly competitive environment, the management wishes to be vigilant towards any barriers that 
can impede the success of the company. Accordingly, the shareholders of RPL passed a special resolution at the Extraordinary General 
Meeting (EGM) of the company to alter the Articles of Association and empower Board of Directors to transfer the shares of any 
shareholder who competes with the business of the company. Mr. Vaibhav, one of the minority shareholders of RPL who was carrying 
on a competing business of manufacturing and marketing a generic drug similar to one of RPL’s generic drug products. He challenged 
the validity of the alteration to be made in the Articles of Association and claimed such action as oppression against minority. 
Protection of Minority Interest
In addition to manufacturing APIs in-house, RPL also procures large volume of API needed to manufacture some of its medicines. 
Qualitycare Limited, one of its major suppliers of API. During F.Y. 2025-26 RPL procured record volumes of API from Qualitycare 
Limited. As a token of appreciation, the company provided RPL, a group free air tickets. The same was en-cashed by RPL for 
R12 lakh in January 2026 and credited to General Reserve Account.
Another supplier, Cure It Limited provided low quality API last year. On account of this, during the current year the supplier 
of raw material has agreed to a settlement of R15 lakhs instead of R20 lakhs. This was not given effect on the running account of 
the supplier.
Transactions with API Suppliers
Ensuring high quality manufacture of Neucare tablets
Neucare tablets are manufactured in Vishakhapatnam factory in Andra Pradesh. In order to maintain high quality production standards, 
RPL manufactures the required Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API, drug molecule which is a key ingredient used in manufacture 
of the final product) at its plant in Nalgonda (Telangana). This API is for the exclusive use of RPL’s facility in Vishakhapatnam to be 
used in the manufacture of Neucare. There is no market sale of this API in India, nor are goods of like kind or quality available within 
India. After conversion, Neucare tablets are sold from the Vishakhapatnam unit.

Annexure 1: Impact of demand variability on supply chain management
Mohan Giri/ Chief Operating Officer, YVL
From: 	
“Mohan Giri” <mohangiri@yvl.com> 
Sent: 	
3rd May 2025 19:00
To: 	
“Reshma Pathak” <reshmap@yvl.com>; “Hari Kumar” <harik@yvl.com>;  
“Tej Prakash” <tejp@yvl.com>; “Nirav Jain” <Niravj@yvl.com>
Cc: 	
YV Giri “ <yvgiri@yvl.com>
Subject: 	 Impact of demand variability on supply chain management
Date: 	
3rd May 2025
Dear Reshma, Hari and Tej,
Let us take the case of “Vitarich” health supplement tablets, which is a general vitamin supplement that can be bought over the counter by 
any user from a pharmacy. During our annual forecasting exercise, we take inputs from (i) sales in the past year and (ii) inputs from stockists 
and CFAs for information about expected market trends in future. Based on this, we determine our sales forecasts for the tablets, which in 
turn determines the production levels and raw material procurement levels for the next year.
Until date, our forecast based on the above exercise was reasonably accurate. Suddenly, in the months from November 2024 to January 2025, 
there was a spike in demand for Vitarich. This was triggered by special discount schemes that retailers (pharmacies) in certain areas offered 
in order to popularize this product and increase sales. As the demand picked up, they started placing bulk orders with wholesalers, who in 
turn did not have sufficient stock to meet the sudden bulk orders. Therefore, in anticipation of sustained increase in future demand, they 
placed larger bulk orders with us for Vitarich. Due to this the production of Vitarich increased more than twice the projected numbers for 
FY 2024-25. However, once the discount scheme period got over in January 2025, the customer demand started tapering and reached regular 
levels thereafter. Ultimately, in hindsight it was found that this spike was driven more by the discount scheme that was temporary in nature 
rather than an actual sustainable demand for the product. Unfortunately, large numbers of Vitarich tablets that we produced in excess, in 
anticipation of sustained future demand remained unsold.
As pharmaceutical companies, we have a product portfolio that has limited shelf life. As per our company’s policy that is in line with current 
industry best practices, our agreement with the stockists allows them to return medicines that are within 3 months of expiry. Vitarich tablets 
have an expiry of 5 months from date of manufacture. This year, almost 30% of our initial sales volume of Vitarich tablets to the stockists 
have been returned either past their expiry or those that are within 3 months of expiry. As per the regulations, we need to destroy the expired 
goods in a safe manner so as to prevent any public health hazard. 
Not just this, in anticipation of growth in future demand, our raw material team procured the compounds needed to manufacture this 
medicine in large quantities in the months of November and December 2024. However, once the discount scheme period got over in January 
2025, the customer demand started tapering. Therefore, the production levels of these tablets also reduced with time. Therefore, the extra 
stock of raw materials that were procured specially for Vitarich have remained unused. 
This pattern of impact of demand variability on inventory has been noticed in few other medicines as well. As managers of marketing 
and sales, production and procurement, you are collectively responsible for this unnecessary production. Please let me know how we can 
collectively resolve such issues.
Thanks,
Mohan Giri
Your Vitality Limited (YVL), a large pharmaceutical company headquartered in Hyderabad, with 
manufacturing facilities in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, operates in a region with a thriving 
pharmaceutical ecosystem. This locational advantage provides access to suppliers, skilled manpower, and 
infrastructure. The company undertakes complex, interconnected activities to deliver medicines safely 
and on time, and Michael Porter’s Value Chain Analysis offers valuable insights into these synergies. 
The case study also highlights the role of Mohan Giri, Chief Operating Officer, who leverages feedback 
from CFAs and stockists to address downstream supply chain issues. A recurring challenge arises from mismatches between demand 
and production, especially for products with limited shelf life. This information asymmetry has, at times, triggered the Bullwhip 
effect, resulting in expired inventory and non-value-added activities such as sales returns, documentation, regulatory compliance for 
destruction, and GST-related issues. These processes consume significant resources and increase costs. Hence, management must 
focus on minimizing such inefficiencies while seeking opportunities to sustain profits. Value chain and supply chain analyses remain 
vital tools in building flexibility and agility.
Operating under competitive pressures also brings ethical challenges. The risk of employee fraud, including revenue misreporting, is 
a critical concern—even senior management may engage in such practices. The case study examines the auditor’s role in recognizing 
these risks, especially when management withholds information. It also considers the procedures under the Companies Act, 2013 for 
dealing with fraud and terminating employees involved in misconduct.
In summary, by understanding how each activity adds value, YVL can avoid inefficiencies, reduce costs, optimize operations, and 
enhance customer satisfaction. Simultaneously, robust performance management and ethical safeguards are essential to prevent 
fraudulent behaviour and protect stakeholder interests.
“We rely on our patents and other proprietary rights to provide exclusive rights to market certain of our products, and if such patents 
and other rights were limited, invalidated or circumvented, our financial results could be materially and adversely affected1.”

The Chartered Accountant Student     October 2025 07
Vivalife is a medicine that is prescribed by cardiologists to treat heart ailments. It has a shelf life of 
9 months from the date of manufacture. On expiry, the pharmacists or stockists who hold the medicine in 
their inventory return it to the upstream supplier, who then eventually returns it to the manufacturer i.e. 
to YVL. As per regulations, YVL is obliged to destroy them in order to prevent any public health hazard 
on consumption of expired medicines. Below are some of the details regarding the medicines returned by 
various stockists to YVL relating to Vivalife medicine that was sold to them during FY 2025-26.
YVL supplied medicines to Health Distributors Pvt. Ltd. and Eagle Distributors Pvt. Ltd. on 
25th April 2025, and both returned the expired medicines on 25th February 2026. Further, medicines were 
supplied to JJ Pharma Distributors and KK Pharma Distributors on 1st July 2025, with the expired stock 
being returned on 20th September 2026 and 20th December 2026, respectively.
Health Distributors Pvt. Ltd. and Eagle Distributors Pvt. Ltd., each considered the return as fresh supply and accordingly issued 
invoice for the return supply. Health Distributors Pvt. Ltd. is a registered person (other than a composition taxpayer) while Eagle 
Distributors Pvt. Ltd  is a composition taxpayer.
With respect to supply to Health Distributors Pvt. Ltd., YVL availed ITC of R25,000 at the time of manufacture of medicines valued 
at R2,50,000. At the time of return of these medicines on account of expiry, ITC available to YVL on the basis of the fresh invoice 
issued by Health Distributors Pvt. Ltd. on return of expired medicines on 25th February 2026 is R30,000. These expired medicines 
were destroyed by YVL on 27th February, 2026. 
Eagle Distributors Pvt. Ltd. is a composition taxpayer. At the time of return of these medicines on account of expiry, the tax as 
applicable based on rates applicable to Eagle Distributors as a composition taxpayer is R10,000 under GST. 
In case of JJ Pharma Distributors and KK Pharma Distributors, on receipt of the expired medicines, YVL has issued a credit note 
for the return of supply of expired medicines. YVL filed its annual return for FY 2025-26 on 5th December, 2026. Again, the expired 
medicines were immediately destroyed on their receipt.
Annexure 2: Case of return of expired medicines
Annexure 3: Suspected fraud in revenue reporting of YVL for FY 2025-26
CA. Aarti Ganesh/ Audit Manager, YVL/ F.Y. 2025-26
From: 	
“Aarti Ganesh” <aartig@kk.com>  
Sent: 	
26th May, 2026 15:30
To: 	
“ Karthik Murthy” <karthikm@kk.com> 
Cc: 	
Subject: 	 Suspected fraud in revenue reporting of YVL for FY 2025-26
Date: 	
26th May 2026
Dear Sir,
As per the accounting policies followed by YVL, revenue from sale of medicines is recognized when control of the goods or service is 
transferred to the stockist (customer) at an amount that reflects the consideration that the company expects to receive. Revenue from 
sale of medicines is recognized net of accrual for sale returns, discounts etc. The estimates for sale returns are complex and requires 
significant judgement and estimation by the company for establishing an appropriate accrual. 
While carrying out our audit procedures for determining the accuracy of reporting of revenue figures, we noticed certain suspicious 
entries. Towards the end of the year, the company reported a spike in the sales of medicines with 8 specific stockists. The goods were 
dispatched, and the sales were recorded as revenue in YVL’s books. Such sales amounted to R50 lakh. Since payment is due after 3 months, 
the corresponding receivable was also recorded. 
However, within the first two weeks of April 2026, the entire sales of R50 lakh were returned to the company. We detected this while 
performing the ageing analysis of accounts receivables as of 31st March 2026. Further, these returns were not considered in the calculations 
while creating the sale return provision for FY 2025-26. The inventory was received, and the accounts receivable was reversed as soon as 
the goods were returned to YVL’s warehouses.
We were unable to get satisfactory answers for the reason for these sale returns from the management. We suspect this to be a case of 
“channel stuffing”, where sales are artificially inflated towards the year end, even though the company knows that the stockists cannot sell 
so much inventory in the near term. Once the year ends, the goods are returned by the stockists. The sales and accounts receivables are 
reversed in the next year. Hence the entire sequence of transactions nets out within a short span of time but spread over different financial 
years. This does indicate an attempt to misstate the revenue and profit for the year. It is an attempt to mislead the investors and other users 
of financial statements. Therefore, it could have potential legal consequences from regulators.
We wish to highlight this audit issue to you at the earliest. Please provide us appropriate guidance on how to proceed further with this 
matter.
Thanks and regards,
Aarti

08 October 2025     The Chartered Accountant Student  
  Question 1
The Board of Directors wish to understand the various activities carried out at YVL in order to gain insights on how 
they can be improved to create better value for customers. EVALUATE the broad set of activities and develop Michael 
Porter’s value chain analysis for YVL.
Answer 1
Michael Porter’s value chain analysis for YVL
A company has a varied mix of activities that can be 
classified as either primary activities or support activities. 
These activities are arranged in a sequential chain that 
will help depict how value (utility) accumulates) for the 
customer. Primary activities are those core operations 
involved in producing, marketing and delivering a product 
to the customer. These activities directly contribute to the 
creation of the product. Support activities help primary 
activities become more efficient. Analysing the value chain 
by breaking down these activities helps a company identify 
where opportunities for improvement lie, thereby aiding in 
creating a competitive advantage 
Primary activities of YVL
Inbound logistics 
In order to manufacture high quality medicines, the Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs), which is the key input needs to be 
of consistent quality and efficacy. YVL has located its manufacturing plants in Hyderabad, Nalgonda and Visakhapatnam that are 
in close proximity of units that can supply this key compound. This has given the company a strategic advantage. This allows the 
company to choose from a wide supplier base, to ensure that it procures API of the required quality in sufficient quantity, which is 
paramount to manufacture of safe medicines. 
Further, raw materials are required to be stored and handled in specific methods. The presence of a thriving pharmaceutical 
industry in this region allows the company to procure or arrange for the needed facilities easily. Similarly, procurement of other 
raw materials like other compounds needed for manufacturing, packaging material for medicines, skilled talent required for the 
company’s operations, necessary infrastructure etc. are easily available in the region. Therefore, location of its plants in Hyderabad, 
Nalgonda and Visakhapatnam ensures that YVL gets access to high quality input raw materials and facilities in sufficient volumes.
Operations 
Medicines manufactured can be in the form of tablets, capsules, injections, liquids etc. to ensure appropriate drug delivery to the 
patient in the correct dosage. The activities also include packaging and labelling to ensure regulatory requirements; quality control 
and assurance to ensure proper safety of the drugs manufactured.
YVL wishes to manufacture high quality medicines following stringent quality norms. Therefore, the entire production is handled 
in-house which can give the company complete control over the quality of medicines. 
Outbound logistics 
YVL caters to both the domestic and international markets. 
For the domestic market, it uses the services of Clearing and Forwarding Agents (CFAs) who facilitate the distribution of medicines 
from the company to various stockists spread across the country. The company has to ensure that distribution channels through 
CFAs reach targeted regions. At the same time, it is also important to ensure that the medicines, while in transit or in the custody 
of CFAs are stored and handled properly to ensure that quality and safety standards are met. Inventory management of the stock of 
medicines with the CFAs is needed to ensure that sales to their customers (stockists) is delivered on time.
Similarly, on account of being a port city, YVL can easily arrange for the export of goods from its plant in Visakhapatnam. 
Marketing and sales 
Product visibility plays a key role in generating sales for YVL. For branded (patented) medicines, a newer customer base / market 
has to be developed in order to generate sales. For generic (non-branded medicines) the need to capture higher market share is 
paramount for generating sales volumes that are needed to maintain profits at sustainable levels. Hence, public awareness about the 
product is important for either type of medicine.
Out-reach to the public through advertisements through television, print and social media helps increase public awareness of the 
YVL’s product portfolio. Popular and catchy taglines like “The Promise of Vitality” improves the visibility of the brand. These are 
important to capture the market share and generate sales. 
Market coverage in also strengthened based on inputs from CFAs, who are in charge of actual distribution improves their market 
reach by identifying potential gaps and onboarding newer stockists. 
Periodic feedback about different medicines, current trends in the market, competitor activity, increasing the clientele all contribute 
to improving YVL’s market reach and thereby increase market share.

IBS
The Chartered Accountant Student     October 2025 11
Unlike conventional subjects that focus primarily on rules, standards, or calculations, the IBS paper encourages students 
to step into the shoes of a decision-maker. In real-life situations, decisions are seldom based on a single dimension; they 
require a balanced approach that considers perspectives such as finance, strategy, ethics, law, taxation, and risk. The paper 
is designed to help students think holistically, integrating knowledge from various disciplines to develop practical and 
insightful solutions in complex business environments. To illustrate this, the case study on the pharmaceutical industry 
discussed here highlights how decisions in areas such as R&D investment, patent protection, regulatory compliance, and 
ethical considerations are interconnected, offering valuable insights into how strategic choices play out in real-world 
practice. Ultimately, the IBS paper aims to prepare students to take on leadership or advisory roles with confidence.
“We make decisions that are in the long-term interest of the business, even if they might have some negative 
short-term impacts. I like to have shareholders who also have that philosophy .”
— Dilip Shanghvi (Founder & MD, Sun Pharma)
CA FINAL - PAPER 6: INTEGRATED BUSINESS SOLUTIONS (IBS) 
Overview
Categories of Medicines 
India the “Pharmacy of the World”
The pharmaceutical industry is unlike any other. Medicine is the restorer of health and life; they can save and prolong lives. Due to 
the direct and immediate impact on public health and safety, trust and integrity have become the cornerstones for the companies 
operating within this industry. Companies that manufacture medicines known as pharmaceutical companies. They discover, 
develop, produce and market medication to treat or alleviate various ailments. 
Some of the renowned pharmaceutical companies in the world include Pfizer Inc., Johnson & Johnson, Merck & Co. Inc., AbbVie 
Inc., AstraZeneca PLC, Eli Lilly and Company, Novartis AG, Sanofi S.A., Briston Myers Squibb Company among many others.
The global pharmaceutical industry is worth about USD 1.6 trillion, with India contributing about 3%-3.5%. The Indian 
Pharmaceutical market is valued at USD 55 billion.  The industry is expected to grow to reach USD 130 billion by 2030 and is 
expected to reach USD 450 billion by 20471.
India is the world’s most populous nation. Hence, the domestic demand for medicines is large. In addition, it is the largest supplier 
of generic medicines providing 20% of the world’s supply and a key player in the affordable vaccines market2. 
Therefore, India has a unique advantage of having an export market that is as large as the domestic market. With over 10,000 
manufacturing facilities, 3,000 pharmaceutical companies and 650 US-FDA-compliant plants – the highest number outside the 
United States1. 
Medicines are categorized as either branded or generic. Pharmaceutical companies invest a lot of money in research and development 
in order to discover newer medicines to treat various medical conditions. Extensive research, clinical trials and eventually regulatory 
approvals are required in order to develop prescription medicines. After regulatory approvals, the companies apply for patents, 
which on approval from the country’s patent office gives the innovator company exclusive rights of the intellectual property as 
also over the manufacture and marketing of the drug. Companies then create public awareness by  investing heavily in marketing 
campaigns. They give these prescription drugs a special name (brand), hence they are known as branded drugs. Some of the well-
known branded drugs are Tylenol (pain and fever reduction owned by McNeil Consumer Healthcare), Advil (Ibuprofen for pain, 
head cold, sleep problems etc. owned by Haleon). Branded medicines are sold at a much higher cost in order to recoup the large 
investment made for research and development and marketing of the medicines.
Generally, the patent is granted from 15 to 20 years. This first-mover advantage ensures that the company gets monopoly over the 
market, and this can yield tremendous profits. Therefore, branded drugs give product differentiation advantage to the company. 
Once the patent expires, any pharmaceutical company can manufacture the generic version of this medicine. Generic medicines 
are created from the similar formulation of a branded medicine with very slight variations. It works in the same way as the branded 
medicine and provides the same clinical benefit. However, generic medicines can enter the market only on the expiry of patent 
restrictions of the original patent. These manufacturers lose out on not having the first mover advantage in the market. However, 
generic medicines can be produced at a very low cost since such a manufacturer does not have to incur costly R&D expenses, 
marketing expenses etc. This low-cost advantage helps generic drug manufacturers remain profitable. Hence, they produce 
medicines in large numbers. Since there is no legal barrier, many companies with similar drug formulation compete within the 
generic medicine market category. India is the leader in global generic medicine market.

3

Some of the renowned pharmaceutical companies in India, that operate on a global scale are Sun Pharmaceutical Industries Ltd., 
Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories Ltd., Cipla Ltd., Zydus Lifesciences Limited, Lupin Limited, Torrent Pharmaceuticals Limited, Divi’s 
Laboratories Limited, Aurobindo Pharma Limited among many others. Many of these companies are located in Gujarat, Telangana, 
Andra Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh and Maharashtra.
Pharmaceutical supply chain has to work with optimum performance to ensure effective delivery of medicines to the end user patient. 
Unlike any other industry, shortage of medicines can cause immediate repercussions on public health. Therefore, adequate level of 
inventory has to be maintained to ensure seamless supply. Due to the nature of the product, medicines have to be stored in proper 
conditions within warehouses that ensure their safety and efficacy. The costs to establish and maintain these specific needs for storage 
and transportation within the entire supply chain are significant. In addition, medicines have a defined shelf life, beyond which the 
company has to incur the cost of expired medicines (waste) that need to be kept at the minimum. The heightened need for optimum 
inventory level management within the supply chain requires close co-ordination among the different stakeholders who manage it. 
A simple version of Pharmaceutical Supply Chain would be as below:
As mentioned above, for companies that focus on developing innovative medicines, research and development costs are exorbitant, 
with slim chances of success of discovery of a new novel drug molecule. A commercially viable branded drug has to be further 
widely marketed in order to generate public awareness that can provide sales traction. Branded drugs that enter the market are 
therefore priced high to recoup these costs. However, since the chances of success of finding a new drug molecule are often times 
very slim, companies succumb to the pressure of having to show results on huge R&D investments. Sometimes the certain technical 
information can be withheld or tampered with in order to show a “falsely successful outcome”. Such unethical practices can cause 
immense harm to public health, many times resulting in tragic deaths or lifelong untreatable medical conditions. This leads to further 
civil and criminal litigation.
On the other hand, generic drug manufacturers face intense competition from having many rivals offering similar medication. 
Working under inflationary conditions and supply chain disruptions caused by external events, pharmaceutical companies have 
to meet many expectations of stakeholders, particularly that of shareholders. Succumbing to such pressures, companies can try to 
inflate the sales revenue for a particular period by pushing excess inventory on distributors and pharmacies beyond their legitimate 
sales needs. This “channel stuffing” is a risk that auditors need to be wary of while performing their audits. 
Good manufacturing practices to provide high quality medicines, good governance that can make healthcare affordable, meeting 
expectations of regulators and other stakeholders while also following sound ethical business practices are core values that every 
pharmaceutical company should imbibe. This will help build sustainable business that earns public trust.
The upstream sourcing for the manufacturer is the suppliers of Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs) and other key materials 
(chemical compounds, medical device suppliers, package and label suppliers etc.) that are needed to manufacture the medicine. 
Pharmaceutical companies manufacture medicines, ready to distribute them to the market. The distribution channel is handled by 
wholesalers (major stockiest), meet the demand generated downstream and replenish stocks from the manufacturer from time to 
time. Further in downstream, the pharmacies provide a vital link to the consumers of the medicines namely end user patients and 
hospitals / health care providers.
The unique feature of this industry is that consumption of medicine is not defined by the end users themselves. Rather it is the 
prescriber (doctors / physicians) and pharmacists who are the main decision makers regarding consumption rather than the end 
user themselves. Demand forecasting is done based on the inputs received from pharmacies and stockiest. Lack of information 
transparency within the supply chain can create disruptions due to demand variability. Changes in demand downstream, which can 
be unpredictable, can cause fluctuations in production and inventory levels upstream. This is called the “Bullwhip effect” within 
the supply chain. While shortage of medicines can have an immediate impact on public health and lost sales opportunities for 
companies, excess inventory can lead to unnecessary costs like increased cost of storage and transportation and waste in the form 
of expired medicines. In addition, external factors such as pandemics, natural disasters, geo-political environment, which are all 
beyond the control of the company can cause severe disruptions to the supply chain. Inefficient supply chains can therefore prove to 
be financially costly to pharmaceutical companies. Therefore, companies are increasingly using technology to integrate the supply 
chain to make it, more efficient, flexible and resilient.

Established 20 years ago, Your Vitality Limited (YVL) is an Indian pharmaceutical company headquartered in Hyderabad. They

executive officer (CEO) of YVL. 
Vision of YVL: “To be a trusted provider of medicines of high quality that improve lives globally.” The company has

Pharmaceutical industry landscape
The company is operating in a highly competitive industry space. Developing branded medicines require 
huge upfront investments in research and development, regulatory compliance and patenting. Once the 
company is granted a patent, it has the ability to charge prices that can help recoup its investment while 
also ensuring profitability. The patent grants the company exclusive rights over the sales, which provides a 
competitive advantage. However, until the patent is granted and the new medicine achieves sufficient sales 
traction, there is a significant risk of not recouping the initial R&D investment.
As for generic medicines, there are many companies that manufacture similar medicines. Due to the availability of substitutes, the 
competition in the generic medicine market is cut-throat. Additionally, margins are under pressure due to inflationary pressures 
from input costs. Therefore, for generic medicines, companies aim to capture large market share in order to generate sales volumes 
that can yield sustainable profits.
Broad set of activities at YVL
There are many bulk drug manufacturers in and around Hyderabad. In fact, in today’s times, 
Hyderabad is known as the bulk drug capital of India and vaccine capital of the world. YVL’s 
decision to locate the plant in Hyderabad and Nalgonda, in the state of Telangana, gave it a 
strategic advantage. Bulk drug manufacturers produce Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients 
(APIs), the main compound based on which the medicine is further developed. Similarly, 
Visakhapatnam is within 600 kilometres from Hyderabad and Nalgonda, in the state of 
Andra Pradesh. In addition to having similar bulk drug manufacturers, who supply API to the

Strategic Insights into the Chemical and Petrochemical (CPC) Industry
Industry Landscape
The Chemical and Petrochemical (CPC) industry holds a pivotal position in an economy as it provides the basic materials required 
for the functioning of other industries. It serves as a reliable indicator of manufacturing trends and supply chain challenges within an 
economy. The CPC industry is vast, encompassing various manufacturing sectors that heavily rely on chemicals. It provides critical 
feedstock to numerous industries, making it indispensable. In India, the chemical industry is highly diversified, covering more than 
80,000 commercial products1. 
The applications of the CPC industry span multiple sectors. In Agriculture and Nutrition, it plays a crucial role by contributing to 
fertilizers and crop protection. In the Pharma sector, it provides essential raw materials for the production of drugs and healthcare 
products. The Building and Construction sector benefits from key components such as adhesives, sealants, and polymers supplied 
by the CPC industry. Furthermore, it supports Mining and Infrastructure through specialized chemicals essential for processing and 
construction activities. In Personal Care and Hygiene, it enables the production of soaps, cosmetics, and sanitizers. The Automotive 
and Transportation sector depends on CPC for high-performance oils and greases, while the Paint and Coatings industry relies on 
raw materials for protective and decorative finishes. Additionally, the Consumer Goods and Electronics sector benefits from CPC 
products like plastics, adhesives, and packaging materials, emphasizing the industry’s indispensability across diverse domains.
This diversity can be broadly classified2 into −
•	
Bulk Chemicals (Commodity Chemicals): Chemicals produced in large quantities but with lower value are considered bulk 
chemicals. They significantly cater to the downstream industries. They are further divided into 3 categories alkali, organic and 
inorganic.
•	
Petro-Chemicals: Also known as petroleum distillates, these chemicals are derived from petroleum and natural gas by refining. 
It includes polymers, and synthetic fibres, performance plastics and others.
•	
Speciality Chemicals: Chemicals with high value but low production volume are considered specialty chemicals like surfactants, 
textile chemicals, paints and coating, dyes, agrochemicals and others. This is highly researched and development-intensive 
category of chemicals. Speciality Chemicals account for more than 50% of the total chemical exports from India.
India’s Chemical and Petrochemical (CPC) industry is worth 220 billion USD and it is expected to grow to about 300 billion USD 
by 20303. India offers a lucrative business ecosystem with favourable investment policies that have attracted global CPC industry, 
converting it into a potential investment region to that plays a pivotal role within the global supply chain. 
Various international and national megatrends, such as shifts in consumer preferences and income demographics, increasing 
digitalization, and innovation, are expected to drive the growth of India’s CPC industry in the coming years.

Agrochemical Industry (Fertilizers/ Crop Nutrition / Speciality Chemicals) 
(a core product in our case studies)
Figure- Supply Chain4
Supply Chain Dynamics 
The supply chain of this industry is a complex and multi-stage process. It involves sourcing of raw materials, transportation, 
manufacturing, distribution and disposal of waste products. Analysing this supply chain is crucial to identify potential bottlenecks, 
inefficiencies and risks in the process and suggest ways to improve it. 
The main stages of supply chain (a simplified generic version for student’s understanding) within this industry are as below:
Agrochemical industry is an important segment of the giant chemical and petrochemical (CPC) industry. Like medicines is to human 
beings, agrochemicals protect plants from insects, pests, diseases, weeds among others, all of which lead to destruction of agricultural 
crops. Given the rising population, agrochemicals play an important role in ensuring food security. It is a highly regulated industry 
with lot of emphasis being placed on product safety.
India is an agrarian economy which needs a significant quantity of crop protection and nutrition products. Catering to food 
requirements of a growing population along with a constraint for availability of arable land has created an insatiable demand for 
high quality crop nutrition chemicals that can improve productivity from agricultural activities. India is emerging as a potential 
hub for production of agrochemicals, it is already a significant exporter of these products. The government places special emphasis 
on ensuring that farmers can get supplies in the form of fertilizers, pesticides, insecticides and other crop nutrition solutions at 
reasonable rates. For this it has subsidy schemes like the Nutrient Based Subsidy (for non-urea products) and separate subsidies 
for urea-based products. It also provides grants to companies/ firms to promote research and development in order to develop less 
hazardous and eco-friendly products.
Snapshot of Value Chain of a Firm in the Agrochemical Industry
The value chain refers to the series of activities a business performs to create and deliver a product or service to the market. It 
includes everything from product conception to final delivery and after-sales service. From forecast and planning to customer 
support, each stage of the value chain contributes to creating innovative, sustainable, and safe agrochemical solutions. By leveraging 
advanced technologies, maintaining rigorous quality standards, and aligning with market trends, agrochemical companies can meet 
the evolving demands of farmers while addressing environmental and regulatory challenges.
Forecasting and Planning −
The industry is characterized by high production and sales volumes. Hence planning and forecasting, in particular demand forecasting 
is the bedrock in ensuring seamless operations. Since these are complex activities, forecasting and planning may take the following 
into account:
Grouping Diverse Products: Grouping products based on types, such as fertilizers, pesticides, and specialty chemicals, allows for more 
accurate demand forecasting and better inventory management. This will help the company identify high performing, fast moving 
products as against slow moving low performing products.
Seasonal Forecasting: The agrochemical industry is heavily influenced by seasons, as different crops require different treatments at 
various growth stages. Seasonal forecasting helps companies prepare for demand spikes, aligning production and distribution with 
planting and harvesting cycles.

Order Book Analysis: Analysing past order data helps predict future demand patterns, identifying trends that can inform production 
planning and inventory management. It also helps improve client management systems.
Trend Analysis: Keeping track of market trends, like increased demand for organic or eco-friendly agrochemicals, allows companies 
to adjust their strategies and invest in relevant R&D. Trend analysis is crucial in a dynamic industry where regulatory changes or 
environmental concerns can shift demand patterns.
R&D Laboratory −
Developing Formulations: Companies make crucial investments in R&D to discover effective, environmentally sustainable and safe 
products for crop nutrition and protection. Along with scientific experiments on chemical compounds, advanced technologies such 
as data science, artificial intelligence, predictive analysis among others are used to design compounds, predict efficacy and toxicity of 
different innovations. Such technologies can aid in company’s efforts to reduce development timelines and costs. 
Approval and Testing: Field trials, toxicity assessments and environmental impact studies are undertaken as part of rigorous testing 
procedures to ensure safety, effectiveness and environmental impact of formulations before they are released. Regulatory approvals 
from authorities (such as the Central Insecticides Board in India) are required to ensure the product meets both national and 
international safety standards.
Patenting: Post approval of a formulation, a company patents it to protect its intellectual property rights. Patents prevent competitors 
from replicating the product for a specified period, which incentivizes innovation and allows for a competitive edge in the market.
Material Procurement −
Approved Supplier and Vendor Selection: Quality, reliability, compliance with health and safety standards and cost-effectiveness are 
critical criteria while choosing suppliers and vendors. Reliable suppliers are required to ensure a steady flow of quality raw materials. 
Long-Term Purchase Agreements: To secure a steady supply and potentially negotiate better rates, long-term agreements with 
suppliers are common. This also helps suppliers plan their own production cycles, which can be beneficial for both parties.
Just-in-Time (JIT) Arrangements: JIT procurement enables companies to receive materials as needed. This helps reduce waste, limit 
exposure of raw materials to potential degradation and minimize inventory costs.
Conformance and Quality Control Inspections: Raw materials should meet required specifications. For this, inspections and audit are 
conducted regularly to reduce the risk of non-compliant or defective material being used in production. 
Material Traceability: It is important to be able to track the origin and movement of raw materials through the supply chain. This 
is crucial for crucial for quality control, regulatory compliance, and in case of recalls or audits. It ensures that any issue at any stage 
within the supply chain can be traced back to its source.
Product Manufacture −
Process Types (Continuous, Batch, or JIT): The type of production will depend on demand, production capacity, storage facility and 
cost considerations. Agrochemical companies may choose continuous (constant production) or batch production (smaller, specific 
quantities). Some may employ JIT production to align manufacturing with demand, reducing storage needs and minimizing waste.
Scalability and Capacity Utilization: In case of fluctuating market demands, the company should be able to scale up or scale down its 
production capacity to ensure that production resources are maximized leading to efficient output and cost management. 
Process Automation: Technology enabled automation of business processes is called process automation. Especially useful while 
performing repetitive tasks, automation improves precision in mixing, processing, and packaging, reducing the risk of human error 
and enhancing efficiency. It also supports scalability, allowing companies to quickly ramp up production when necessary and can 
help transform business processes.
Maintenance: Maintaining peak performance of assets and equipment requires scheduled maintenance at regular intervals. This 
is essential for efficient operations, upkeep of equipment, prevent breakdowns and ensure consistent production quality. They 
minimize downtime and improve operational longevity.
Quality Control and Inspection: Due to the hazardous nature of many of its products, agrochemical companies are carrying out 
stringent quality checks, ensuring adherence to regulatory and company standards. Analytical testing, such as chemical composition 
analysis and stability testing, helps ensure product efficacy and safety.
Inventory Management and Distribution −
Warehouse Management: Receiving, storing, packing and shipping products are the day-to-day processes in warehouse management. 
These vital behind the scene activities ensure on-time delivery to customers. Warehouse management systems should optimize use 
of warehouse space to store maximum inventory, it should be easy for staff to find the required inventory, accurate and efficient order 
fulfilment, co-ordinating with suppliers and transportation companies so that materials arrive and orders ship on time. Efficient 
management of these activities improves productivity while keeping the costs low.
Storing and Handling Hazardous Goods: Since agrochemicals can be hazardous, specialized storage facilities with proper ventilation, 
temperature control, and spill containment are necessary. Minimizing accumulation of expiring products through better inventory 
management. Staff must also be trained in the safe handling of chemicals to ensure safety and regulatory compliance.
Inventory Traceability and Expiry: Inventory management systems help track expiration dates and ensure proper rotation of stock. 
Traceability ensures any issues with a batch can be quickly isolated, which is especially crucial in the case of hazardous or sensitive 
chemicals. Use barcode, QR code, or RFID technology for accurate and efficient track and trace across the supply chain. Traceability 
is also important to combat the grey market where spurious products are sold. 
Packing and Dispatch: Proper packaging is essential to maintain product integrity during transportation. Packing protocols are 
followed to protect against damage, leaks, and contamination. Efficient dispatch processes help reduce lead times, ensuring timely 
delivery to customers.

Synopsis of Dakshin Fertilizers and Petrochem Ltd. (DFPL) 
Headquartered in Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala, DFPL’s main manufacturing facility is in Eloor, Ernakulam, along with additional 
plants in Dahej (Gujarat), Hisar (Haryana) and Brahmapur (Odisha). The company is a leading producer of industrial chemicals, 
crop nutrition and mining chemicals.
Backward integration: Despite strong financial results for FY 2023-24 (revenue of R12,000 crores and 60% increase in expected 
profits compared to the previous year), the company continues to face supply chain disruptions and huge volatility in import prices 
of ammonia. In order to build an agile and resilient supply chain that can also aid operational efficiencies, the management has 
taken a strategic decision to set up an ammonia manufacturing plant within DFPL’s main manufacturing complex at Eloor. With a 
capacity of 1,500 MTPD, the piped ammonia will be supplied directly to the finished goods manufacturing unit within the same 
complex. The advantages of this project are summarized include: 
(i)	 Backward integration allows for better realignment of supply chain, developing operational efficiencies that ensure seamless 
production of its core products 
(ii)	 Forex savings due to import substitution and 
(iii)	Cost efficiencies due to reduced storage, transportation and logistics costs. 
The initial capital expenditure is estimated to be around R2,000 crores, for which purpose DFPL decides to borrow an additional 
sum of R1,500 crores from the company’s bankers by following the due procedure as per Companies Act, 2013. In order to establish 
better credibility with the bankers, CA. Fiona, the proprietor of FRP & Co., the statutory auditors of DFPL, has been approached 
by DFPL to have the prospective financial information examined. She must now decide whether she can get involved in such an 
examination. In order to complete the legal formalities relating to the project, DFPL hired Y & E law firm for a consolidated fee of 
R10,00,000. The work was completed by Y&E within 30 days. Ms. Aditi Singh who has been appointed as an Independent Director 
in Aug’24 at DFPL is also a partner at Y&E law firm. The law firm has an annual turnover of less than R1 crore. Post sanctioning of 
additional loan of R1,500 crores, the case study provides the timeline for utilization of these funds towards the project. This would 
determine the capitalization of borrowing costs (Ind AS 23).
Environment sustainability and CSR initiatives: From a strategic perspective, the selling price of the product should support long-
term profitability and competitiveness. To do this, the management explores incorporating environment costs into pricing. For two 
of the main types of fertilizers, Grade A and Grade B that the crop nutrition business unit of DFPL produces, information is provided 
cost centre wise about the cost incurred to produce them. Further information regarding the disposal of solid waste (generated 
during production) using incinerator is also provided in the case study. It explores how the unit head of the crop nutrition business 
would like to incorporate this information, to rework the pricing of each grade of fertilizer depending on their environmental 
impact. DFPL has undertaken several CSR initiatives. These include vendor management adhering to ethical labour practices, 
using technology to mitigate risks posed to the environment from ammonia emissions, increasing share of environmentally friendly 
fertilizers. To get information on these initiatives and their impact, the management uses Triple Bottom Line Reporting Framework. 
Many of the Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) included in this report are non-financial metrics.

Synopsis of Crop Yield Private Limited (CYPL) 
In continuation to case study above, CYPL is established as a Joint Venture between Dakshin Fertilizers and Petrochem Ltd. (DFPL) 
and Greenspan Gmbh at Gopalpur, Odisha. Greenspan Gmbh, widely recognized for its advanced fertilizer technologies and energy 
efficient manufacturing processes, would provide the technical assistance to CYPL. This is extremely beneficial for DFPL’s strategic 
expansion plans to expand its reach in the eastern cost. Meanwhile, by partnering with a domestically reputed company like DFPL, 
Greenspan would be able to establish its presence in India.
As outlined above, the locational advantage of being in close vicinity to Gaspro India Limited (GIL), Gopalpur, its main supplier 
of natural gas along with developing cost efficiencies by operating on a larger scale with a planned capacity of 10,00,000 MT per 
year are the key benefits of this strategic decision. Both parties have hired Pro International (PI), to guide with legal and regulatory 
compliance, facilitating establishment of the manufacturing facility and providing management consulting service to ensure smooth 
operations and strategic alignment. 
Establishing of CYPL: Since natural gas is a key raw material in the production of fertilizers, the company entered into a 5-year 
long-term contract with GIL, Gopalpur. GIL will be the sole supplier of this critical raw material. Land worth R100 crores has been 
procured in Gopalpur to set up CYPL. Machineries from DFPL’s erstwhile Brahmapur facility, along with imported machineries 
from subsidiary of Greenspan Gmbh will form part of the total plant and machinery of CYPL. Since these require constant 
maintenance, CYPL has entered into short term contracts for factory consumables, primary tools and maintenance equipment to 
be supplied by small enterprises located in Gopalpur. 
Resistance to CYPL’s establishment and labour unrest at Brahmapur: During project implementation, CYPL faces resistance 
from the local public who feel that the company’s location within 1 kilometre of the town’s public settlements in a densely populated 
area could result in concerns about public health safety. This stems from a recent gas leak incident from a similar fertilizer plant in 
Paradip, Odisha. More than 1,000 residents from Gopalpur and Brahmapur gathered to protest against the establishment of CYPL 
in the location, albeit it being approved by the government after complying with necessary regulations. Relocation would entail 
establishing CYPL 600 kms. away, effectively making the project unviable on both operational and cost considerations. Similarly, 
there is resistance from the workers at DFPL’s Brahmapur facility, spearheaded by their workers’ union, who are unhappy with the 
compensation package being offered by the company to relocate to CYPL’s facility at Gopalpur. These issues can also come under 
the radar of government regulatory authorities and company shareholders both in India and Germany.
There is a very real risk of these developments snowballing into a huge public outcry, that can be disastrous for both operations 
and reputation of DFPL and Greenspan Gmbh. Hence, Mr. Venkata Ravi (Chairman of DFPL) and Mr. Gerhard Braun (Managing 
Director of Greenspan Gmbh) approach Mr. Jeevan Sampath (partner at Pro International) to effectively handle the situation. 
The case study discusses how PI makes use of Mendelow’s Matrix to guide CYPL to effectively handle each of the stakeholders 
influencing this issue. Eventually an amicable settlement is reached with the disgruntled workers while all issues relating to public 
resistance are addressed and resolved. Production at CYPL’s Gopalpur facility commences on January 1, 2025.
Strategic expansion: Gaspro India Limited (GIL) is the main supplier of natural gas to DFPL’s unit at Brahmapur, Odisha. 
Incidentally, GIL is setting up a Liquified Natural Gas (LPG) receipt facility at Gopalpur. DFPL finds this an opportunity to increase 
its market presence in Odisha and northern belt of Andra Pradesh by setting up a fertilizer manufacturing unit at Gopalpur. This 
strategic decision is taken due to the locational advantages that CYPL can have by being in close vicinity to Gaspro India Limited 
(GIL) at Gopalpur. This increases the ability to scale up operations and the venture can benefit from economies of scale. The new 
unit, Crop Yield Private Limited (CYPL) will be a joint venture with Greenspan Gmbh. DFPL’s unit at Brahmapur will be shut down 
following the establishment of CYPL at Gopalpur. Following this the machineries will then be transferred to CYPL. In addition, 
machineries with better technology and larger capacities will also be imported from one of Greenspan Gmbh’s subsidiaries in 
Germany. As part of project planning, the case study highlights the need to consider tax planning that can be done by claiming 
certain investment linked tax incentives that are available to specified businesses as contained in the Income Tax Act, 1961. 
Corporate governance and accountability: The case study highlights the number of strategic initiatives that the management of 
DFPL has to take to navigate this challenging industry landscape. It is important to have professionals with expertise in diverse fields 
as part of the company’s Board of Directors in order to have a strong corporate governance. Appointments and reappointments 
to various positions of key management personnel should be based on proper performance evaluation and in conformance with 
the regulations. Many of the key management personnel render their expertise during the course of their tenure, for which they 
may be adequately compensated in the form of professional fees. The case study highlights the importance of adhering to proper 
procedures to ensure compliance with laws and regulations, particularly under the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI regulations. All 
of this has an immense bearing on the ability, quality and effectiveness of strategic decisions made by a company. 
Corporate governance involves overseeing business strategies while ensuring fiscal accountability, ethical corporate behaviour, 
fairness to both internal and external stakeholders. Accountability extends to statutory auditors as well, who as a part of their 
role are privy to sensitive and confidential information about the company. Accountability for decisions and ethical corporate 
responsibility can boost stakeholder confidence.
Students should read FY 2024-25 as 2023-24 and FY 2023-24 as 2022-23 in the first paragraph, where Mr. Venkata 
Ravi, Chairman of DFPL, addresses the board. The R1,600 Crores from EFF is for FY 2023-24, and the AGM is on 9th Sept’ 2024.

IBS  
08
February 2025     The Chartered Accountant Student  
Supply Disruption and subsequent scaling down of operations at CYPL: On September 30,2025 following a massive fire at 
GIL’s underground natural gas pipeline at Arjyapalli, Odisha, 15 people tragically lost their lives and there was significant damage 
to property in that area. Thereby for safety reasons GIL was forced to halt supply of natural gas through its pipelines in Odisha. 
Extensive repair of its pipelines and safety tests were conducted across the entire pipeline network originating from its LNG facility. 
While the technical team at GIL worked on this, supply was completely suspended due to which many of its customers including 
CYPL suffered significant losses due to unexpected stoppage of a critical raw material. To maintain operations at a minimum scale, 
in October 2025 Mr. Ramakant Bhushan, Managing Director of CYPL entered into another 5-year fixed price contract with Natural 
Gas Suppliers Limited (NGSL), a competitor of GIL. However, NGSL’s limited capability of meeting CYPL’s entire requirement 
of natural gas, inability to find other alternate suppliers forced the company to scale down its operations. In place of GIL, NGSL 
became CYPL’s supplier of natural gas. This highlights the critical need for managing the upstream supplier chain to address 
unforeseen exigencies.
Going concern issues at CYPL: Since the cost structure consisted majorly of fixed costs that need to be incurred regardless of scale 
of operations, CYPL lost its cost efficiencies. Financial instability impacted CYPL’s ability to enter and terminate contracts with 
suppliers. Due to regulatory constraints governed by the government’s subsidy mechanism and market competition, the company 
could not pass on the increased cost of production to customers. Fertilizers were sold at a loss thereby straining its financial 
position. CYPL established a recovery committee comprising of key management personnel as well as invited Mr. Jeevan Sampath 
to provide consulting services in this regard. Strategic tools such as the Altman’s Z-score were used to assess CYPL’s financial 
stability and take appropriate measures to address them.
CA. Bharat Chowdhary, the statutory auditor had to carefully assess the issue of going concern at CYPL, at the time of issuing the 
audit report for the financial year 2025-26.
Additional capital infusion, optimally utilizing the subsidy support from the government and market repositioning were all part of 
the multi-pronged strategy that eventually were undertaken to stabilize operations at CYPL. Eventually in March 2028, almost 30 
months after the tragic accident, GIL resumed supply of natural gas to CYPL. Due to GIL, Gopalpur’s ability to meet the entirety of 
its natural gas requirements, CYPL renewed its business with the supplier by entering into a fresh contract. This will enable CYPL 
to scale back its operations to originally planned levels as decided at the time of its inception. This also led to CYPL prematurely 
cancelling its contract with NGSL. GIL once again became CYPL’s sole supplier of natural gas. The case study highlights that the 
impact that supply chain management decisions can have on the long-term sustainability and profitability of business.
Performance assessment of Mr. Ramakant Bhushan, Managing Director at CYPL: Due to the extra-ordinary nature of business 
environment at CYPL, rather than focusing on financial metrics alone, the performance assessment of Mr. Ramakant Bhushan for 
the financial years 2025-26 to 2027-28 had to also be based on many non-financial metrics like building supply chain resilience, 
improving market share, improving sales, reducing costs.
Indirect tax a significant component of CYPL’s cost structure: The profitability of the company is significantly influenced by the 
tax structure. Regarding the Goods and Services Tax (GST), the case study includes a discussion on the inverted duty structure, 
the determination of the value of supply for GST on fertilizers that receive government subsidies, and GST on the procurement 
of natural gas. Additionally, CYPL relies heavily on imports for its raw material requirements. The case study also explores the 
company’s liability and rights concerning customs duty payments in cases where raw materials are pilfered while in the custody of 
Port Trusts, which act as custodians.
Based on real life scenarios within this highly regulated agrochemical industry, the above case studies bring out a series of 
interconnected issues that need to be tackled often time simultaneously in order to build a profitable and sustainable business. 
Businesses do not work in silos, the decision taken in one area can impact another. Often business leaders need to consider not 
just the financial aspects but also the non-financial aspects as well. For example, the establishment of CYPL in Gopalpur, Odisha 
not only made financial sense due to the cost advantages it offered, but also leveraged the capability of scaling up operations (a 
non-financial consideration) due to proximity to GIL, the supplier of its key raw material. This decision simultaneously resulted 
in other issues that the management had to tackle namely labour unrest at Brahmapur facility of DFPL as well as public resistance 
to establishment of CYPL at Gopalpur. Therefore, it requires the management, who is the decision maker to have a complete, 
holistic view of business rather than having a restricted view of only profitability of the venture. Therefore, business decisions 
should be based on strategic objectives. Decisions that can build dexterity and agility in business operations can be effective 
in having a positive impact on productivity, profitability and long-term growth. In today’s scenario, sustainability of business 
also depends on having a healthy business eco-system which requires business decisions to be compliant with various laws and 
regulations, be agile to supply chain disruptions, have sustainable business models that take care of environmental, societal 
and corporate governance issues. Only then will the company be able to garner stakeholder confidence that can significantly 
influence its brand image.
KEY TAKEWAYS

CA FINAL - PAPER-6: INTEGRATED BUSINESS SOLUTIONS
“Good business leaders create a vision, articulate the vision, passionately  
own the vision, and relentlessly drive it to completion.”
– Jack Welch, Former CEO of General Electric
Solving multidisciplinary ‘Case Study’ will enhance analytical skills and decision-making skills of students. Tis holistic and 
integrated approach ensures that students emerge well-equipped to tackle the challenges presented in the constantly changing business 
environment.
Business decisions, both short-term and long-term, are based on strategic objectives. Eﬀective decisions are those that 
have a positive impact on productivity & proﬁtability and enhance the growth prospects of a business. Eﬀective decision 
making requires the decision maker to consider a complete, holistic view of the business rather than having a siloed 
approach. Business does not work in silos, it is integrated and interconnected where decisions taken in one area can have 
a signiﬁcant impact on other areas. Considering these principles, students are encouraged to integrate their professional 
values, practical work experience, and knowledge gained from speciﬁc academic studies. Te goal is to cultivate a skillset 
capable of crafting well-organized, integrated business solutions. 
Integral to the Integrated Business Solutions (IBS) is the ‘Case Study’, a vital aspect of the CA Final Level. Here, students 
must apply their knowledge gathered from the ﬁve core subjects − Financial Reporting, Advanced Financial Management, 
Advanced Auditing, Assurance and Professional Ethics, Direct Tax Laws & International Taxation, Indirect Tax Laws; and 
Self-paced Modules Set A & B. In this journal, we are focussing on those case studies which involve making of ‘strategic 
decisions’. Each ‘Case Study’ unfolds a unique business situation, presenting a scenario complete with mission, vision, 
objectives, challenges, key stakeholders, and relevant data. Te strategic aspects have been discussed in detail in the 
answers solely for enhancing your understanding of the concepts. Concept insights have been incorporated at the relevant 
places. Tese case studies are in addition to the case studies webhosted at the BoS Knowledge Portal at URL: https://
boslive.icai.org/sm_chapter_details.php?p_id=18&m_id=74. Te aim is to provide a variety of case studies covering 
diﬀerent subjects at Final Level and Set A & Set B. Students are advised to work out the case studies webhosted at the 
portal at the above link and case studies given in the journal to understand the manner of integration of diﬀerent subjects 
in solving a ‘Case Study’. 
Strategic decision-making involves a meticulous analysis of the business model and subsequent strategic adaptations. 
Decisions may range from new product development and market exploration to considering diversiﬁcation, whether in 
related or unrelated areas. Te choice between related and unrelated areas presents challenges, as stakeholders may resist 
the later due to perceived risks, potentially impacting market capitalization. In the case of a strategic shift towards a 
related area, exploration of options such as horizontal integration or vertical integration (whether forward or backward 
integration) in the supply chain is crucial. 
Tese strategic moves require a lot of ﬁnancial decisions. In addition to that there is need of robust ﬁnancial risk 
management system. Moreover, proper adherence to accounting standard, tax laws and other statutory compliances under 
the various corporate legislations are fundamental to the strategic decision. Adhering to these standards ensures legal 
compliance, shielding the company from legal repercussions and ﬁnes. It also aids management in allocating resources 
eﬃciently and evaluating the performance of various business units or projects based on reliable ﬁnancial data. 
On top of that, good corporate governance, fostering ethical business practices, inﬂuences an organization’s strategy and 
performance. Tis emphasis on ethics is essential not only for business organisations but also for CAs, as stakeholders 
place enormous conﬁdence in their role. Te increasing instances of corporate frauds and subsequent failures, with ripple 
eﬀects on economies, have increased the responsibilities of CAs to ensure that organizations discharge their reporting 
responsibilities diligently.
Hence, the integrated approach advocated in Core Paper-6 at the CA Final Level emphasizes the importance of considering 
interrelated issues spanning ﬁnance, accounting standards, assurance, direct tax laws, indirect tax laws, company law, and 
SEBI compliances alongside strategic decision making.
